questions.prompt: What defines an element?
options: Only one atom in the entire sample
Any substance containing two types of atom
questions.explanation: An element is defined by atomic type, not sample size or colour.

questions.prompt: Which is a compound?
questions.explanation: Water has different elements chemically bonded in a fixed composition.

questions.prompt: Which is a molecular element?
questions.explanation: O₂ contains only oxygen atoms in discrete molecules.

questions.prompt: Why is solid NaCl not described as separate NaCl molecules?
options: It contains no atoms or ions.
It is an extended ionic lattice.
questions.explanation: NaCl describes the ratio of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in the lattice.

questions.prompt: What is copper metal made of structurally?
options: Separate Cu₂ molecules in ordinary bulk copper
Water molecules with a copper colour
Only Cu²⁺ ions with no electrons
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding involves positive metal centres and delocalised electrons.

questions.prompt: Which sample is a mixture?
questions.explanation: Brass is an alloy mixture of copper and zinc, not a fixed-formula compound.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a compound from a mixture?
options: It can contain only one element.
It must always be a gas.
Its elements are chemically combined in fixed proportions.
It is separated by ordinary filtration into its elements.
questions.explanation: Compounds have defined chemical composition; mixtures have variable composition.

questions.prompt: Graphite is best described as…
options: a molecular compound of carbon and oxygen.
a mixture of carbon and sodium.
an element with a giant covalent layered structure.
questions.explanation: Graphite contains carbon only, in extended covalent layers.

questions.prompt: Which statement about molecules is correct?
options: Some elements are molecular and some compounds are molecular.
Every compound consists of discrete molecules.
Every element is monatomic in every state.
Molecule and mixture mean the same thing.
questions.explanation: O₂ is a molecular element and H₂O a molecular compound, unlike metallic Cu and ionic NaCl.

questions.prompt: What changes when a physical mixture is made?
options: Every component must become a new element.
Substances are combined without necessarily forming new chemical bonds between components.
The mixture must acquire a fixed molecular formula.
questions.explanation: Physical mixing does not by itself create a fixed-ratio compound.

questions.prompt: What carries electrical charge through a solid metal?
options: Free-moving positive metal ions through the solid
questions.explanation: Delocalised electrons are mobile; the metal ions occupy the lattice.

questions.prompt: What holds a metallic structure together?
options: Covalent bonds only between pairs of isolated metal molecules
Attraction between positive metal centres and delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Electrostatic metallic bonding extends throughout the structure.

questions.prompt: Why can many metals be bent without shattering?
options: Layers can move while metallic bonding remains.
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding can persist as layers or dislocations move.

questions.prompt: Which is a conducting non-metal?
options: Diamond in the ordinary insulating comparison
questions.explanation: Graphite has delocalised electrons within its layers.

questions.prompt: Why does solid NaCl not conduct by ion movement?
options: Its ions are held in fixed lattice positions.
questions.explanation: It contains ions, but they are not mobile in the solid.

questions.prompt: Why can molten NaCl conduct?
questions.explanation: Mobile ions carry charge through the melt.

questions.prompt: Which property helps make copper suitable for wires?
options: A tendency to dissolve in cold pure water instantly
Being a molecular gas at room temperature
questions.explanation: Copper conducts and can be drawn into thin wires.

questions.prompt: Why is conduction alone not enough to classify a sample as a metal?
options: Some non-metals such as graphite also conduct.
Conduction proves the sample is an ionic compound.
questions.explanation: Use several properties and structural evidence rather than a single observation.

questions.prompt: In a solid metal connected to a battery, which description is best?
options: The entire positive-ion lattice flows down the wire.
All atoms move at light speed.
Electrons drift while the lattice ions remain near their positions.
The wire must melt before any charge moves.
questions.explanation: Conduction is distinct from bulk movement of the lattice.

questions.prompt: Which statement about metal properties is most accurate?
options: Every metal has exactly the same melting point.
Every shiny solid must be a metal.
Common trends have exceptions, so test and specify the material.
questions.explanation: Properties vary; for example, only some metals show strong ferromagnetism.

questions.prompt: What products form when sodium reacts with water?
options: Sodium oxide and carbon dioxide only
questions.explanation: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.

questions.prompt: How does reactivity generally change down Group 1?
options: It is exactly zero for all members.
questions.explanation: The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded.

questions.prompt: Why is potassium generally more reactive with water than lithium?
options: Lithium gains two electrons more readily.
Its outer electron is lost more readily.
questions.explanation: Increased shielding and distance make electron loss easier down Group 1.

questions.prompt: How does halogen reactivity generally change down Group 17?
options: It is identical for all members.
questions.explanation: Attraction for an incoming electron weakens down the group.

questions.prompt: Which reaction is expected?
questions.explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine and iodine.

questions.prompt: Which is a typical transition-element feature?
options: Variable oxidation states in many compounds
Violent cold-water reaction in every case
questions.explanation: Many transition elements show variable oxidation states.

questions.prompt: Which halogen is a red-brown liquid at ordinary room temperature?
questions.explanation: Bromine is liquid; chlorine and fluorine are gases and iodine is a solid at ordinary room temperature.

questions.prompt: Which statement about transition-metal catalysts is correct?
options: A catalyst must be used up in the overall reaction.
Catalysts change the identities of elements.
Many transition elements or their compounds can act as catalysts.
questions.explanation: Catalysts provide alternative pathways and are regenerated overall; their effects are reaction-specific.

questions.prompt: Why do Group 1 and halogen reactivity trends run in opposite directions?
options: Group 1 reactions involve electron loss, while halogen reactions involve electron gain.
Both groups have exactly the same electron-transfer role.
Every atom gains and loses all its electrons at once.
questions.explanation: Shielding and distance affect electron loss and gain differently.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is justified by no iodine displacement from bromide?
options: Iodine is less reactive than bromine in this comparison.
All halogen displacement reactions are impossible.
questions.explanation: A less reactive halogen cannot oxidise the halide of a more reactive one under the stated comparison.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral formula of magnesium chloride?
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral formula of aluminium oxide?
questions.explanation: Two Al³⁺ balance three O²⁻.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral formula of calcium nitrate?
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻ ions, kept together in brackets.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral formula of sodium sulfate?
questions.explanation: Two Na⁺ balance SO₄²⁻.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral formula of iron(II) chloride?
questions.explanation: Iron(II) means Fe²⁺, requiring two Cl⁻.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral formula of iron(III) oxide?
questions.explanation: Two Fe³⁺ balance three O²⁻.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral formula of copper(II) hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Two OH⁻ groups balance Cu²⁺.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral formula of potassium carbonate?
questions.explanation: Two K⁺ balance CO₃²⁻.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral formula of ammonium sulfate?
questions.explanation: Two NH₄⁺ balance SO₄²⁻.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral formula of magnesium nitride?
questions.explanation: Three Mg²⁺ balance two N³⁻.

questions.prompt: Which metal is most reactive in Mg, Zn, Fe and Cu?
questions.explanation: The simplified order is Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu.

questions.prompt: Which metal lies below hydrogen in this list?
questions.explanation: Copper does not release H₂ from dilute non-oxidising HCl.

questions.prompt: What gas forms when zinc reacts with excess dilute HCl?
questions.explanation: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.

questions.prompt: Which equation represents iron with dilute HCl?
questions.explanation: Iron(II) chloride is the salt in this comparison.

questions.prompt: Why can an aluminium sample react more slowly than its position suggests?
options: A protective surface oxide can impede the reaction.
Aluminium is always below copper in the series.
It has no tendency to form ions.
Reaction rate never depends on the surface.
questions.explanation: Passivation can mask the reactivity of the underlying metal.

questions.prompt: Which comparison marker in the school reactivity series is not a metal?
questions.explanation: Carbon is included as an extraction comparison marker; hydrogen is another non-metal marker.

questions.prompt: What should be controlled in a fair metal–acid rate comparison?
options: Only the colour of the test-tube rack
Acid concentration, temperature and surface-area conditions
questions.explanation: These variables influence observed reaction speed.

questions.prompt: Equal masses of magnesium and zinc produce different final H₂ volumes with excess acid. What must you consider?
options: That one gas is necessarily oxygen
That equal mass always means equal moles
questions.explanation: Compare moles and stoichiometry when interpreting total gas amount.

questions.prompt: What is the main chemical tendency represented by a metal reactivity comparison?
options: Tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions under the comparison
Tendency to gain protons into the nucleus
The exact rate in every possible experiment
questions.explanation: Reactivity is connected to oxidation tendency; conditions still matter.

questions.prompt: Why is dilute nitric acid not interchangeable with dilute HCl for every “metal + acid gives H₂” prediction?
options: Nitric acid is an oxidising acid and can give different reduction products.
Hydrogen is always the only possible gas from every acid.
questions.explanation: The simple hydrogen prediction is for appropriate non-oxidising acid conditions.

questions.prompt: A clean Mg strip is placed in an aqueous solution containing Cu²⁺ ions. What does the simplified reactivity model predict?
options: Sulfate or another spectator anion becomes the metal.
Mg is oxidised and Cu metal deposits.
questions.explanation: The comparison is Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu. Mg is more reactive, so displacement is predicted.

questions.prompt: A clean Zn strip is placed in an aqueous solution containing Cu²⁺ ions. What does the simplified reactivity model predict?
options: Sulfate or another spectator anion becomes the metal.
Zn is oxidised and Cu metal deposits.
questions.explanation: The comparison is Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu. Zn is more reactive, so displacement is predicted.

questions.prompt: A clean Fe strip is placed in an aqueous solution containing Cu²⁺ ions. What does the simplified reactivity model predict?
options: Fe is oxidised and Cu metal deposits.
Sulfate or another spectator anion becomes the metal.
questions.explanation: The comparison is Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu. Fe is more reactive, so displacement is predicted.

questions.prompt: A clean Cu strip is placed in an aqueous solution containing Zn²⁺ ions. What does the simplified reactivity model predict?
options: Sulfate or another spectator anion becomes the metal.
questions.explanation: The comparison is Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu. Cu is not more reactive than the dissolved metal.

questions.prompt: A clean Zn strip is placed in an aqueous solution containing Mg²⁺ ions. What does the simplified reactivity model predict?
options: Sulfate or another spectator anion becomes the metal.
questions.explanation: The comparison is Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu. Zn is not more reactive than the dissolved metal.

questions.prompt: A clean Mg strip is placed in an aqueous solution containing Zn²⁺ ions. What does the simplified reactivity model predict?
options: Sulfate or another spectator anion becomes the metal.
Mg is oxidised and Zn metal deposits.
questions.explanation: The comparison is Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu. Mg is more reactive, so displacement is predicted.

questions.prompt: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which species gains electrons?
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu is reduction.

questions.prompt: What role do sulfate ions play when zinc displaces copper from CuSO₄?
options: They are reduced to copper metal.
They are the only electron donors.
questions.explanation: Sulfate remains aqueous and unchanged in the simplified ionic reaction.

questions.prompt: Why does a copper coating appear on iron in CuSO₄?
options: Copper atoms are created from sulfate.
Iron changes its atomic number to copper.
Cu²⁺ gains electrons from the oxidised iron.
The beaker supplies new copper nuclei.
questions.explanation: Iron is oxidised and dissolved copper ions are reduced.

questions.prompt: Can a copper strip displace copper from its own Cu²⁺ solution as a net reaction?
options: Yes; it must double the copper amount.
Yes; all Cu²⁺ must become zinc.
No; there is no net displacement of itself.
questions.explanation: The same metal/ion pair does not give the proposed net competition reaction.

questions.prompt: Which reducing gas is central to the blast-furnace reduction of iron oxide?
questions.explanation: CO removes oxygen from iron oxides.

questions.prompt: Which equation is balanced for iron(III) oxide reduction by CO?
questions.explanation: Three CO molecules accept the three oxygen atoms from Fe₂O₃.

questions.prompt: Why can carbon be used to extract some metals from oxides?
options: It is more reactive than every metal.
It turns into every extracted metal.
It can remove oxygen from oxides of less reactive metals under suitable conditions.
It eliminates the need for energy.
questions.explanation: The reactivity comparison helps identify suitable reduction routes.

questions.prompt: Why is aluminium not normally extracted by carbon reduction?
options: Carbon reduction works equally for every oxide.
Aluminium oxide is too stable for that route in the usual school comparison.
questions.explanation: Aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series.

questions.prompt: What is the usual industrial route to aluminium?
options: Electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite
Filtering aluminium oxide from water to obtain metal
Distilling the oxide at room temperature
Adding dilute HCl to turn the oxide into metal
questions.explanation: Electrical energy drives reduction of Al³⁺ in the molten electrolyte.

questions.prompt: What is limestone used for in a blast furnace?
options: Producing CaO to remove silica as slag
Acting as the only reducing metal
questions.explanation: CaCO₃ decomposes; CaO reacts with SiO₂ to form calcium silicate slag.

questions.prompt: Which slag-forming equation is correct?
questions.explanation: Basic calcium oxide reacts with acidic silica.

questions.prompt: In CuO reduction by carbon, what happens to copper?
options: Copper remains oxide while only its colour changes.
questions.explanation: Oxygen removal corresponds to reduction of the metal ion.

questions.prompt: Why might an extraction route that is chemically possible still not be chosen industrially?
options: Energy, cost, ore composition and environmental factors also matter.
Every possible route costs the same.
questions.explanation: Practical process selection goes beyond chemical feasibility alone.

questions.prompt: What is oxidised in Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂?
options: Both iron and carbon are reduced
questions.explanation: Carbon goes from +2 in CO to +4 in CO₂, while iron is reduced.

questions.prompt: What is an alloy?
options: A pure element with a fixed atomic number only
A mixture containing at least one metal
questions.explanation: Alloys are metallic mixtures whose compositions can vary.

questions.prompt: What are the principal components of brass?
questions.explanation: Brass is a copper–zinc alloy.

questions.prompt: What are the principal components of bronze?
questions.explanation: Bronze is a copper–tin alloy in this standard comparison.

questions.prompt: What is the base metal in carbon steel?
questions.explanation: Carbon steel is mainly iron with a small amount of carbon.

questions.prompt: Why can adding a different-sized atom make a metal harder?
options: It can hinder layer or dislocation motion.
It makes all atoms identical in size.
questions.explanation: Distortion can impede deformation.

questions.prompt: Why is stainless steel resistant to corrosion?
options: It cannot react under any conditions.
It is made entirely of copper.
Chromium supports a protective oxide film.
questions.explanation: A chromium-rich passive film protects the surface; conditions still matter.

questions.prompt: Why might an alloy be chosen instead of a pure metal?
options: Its combination of properties may better suit the use.
Every alloy is always cheaper and better in every way.
questions.explanation: Hardness, corrosion resistance, conductivity and processability involve trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Which statement about alloy composition is correct?
options: It must always have a single fixed formula.
Its composition can vary and affect its properties.
questions.explanation: Steel can contain carbon; alloy composition and processing are important.

questions.prompt: Why is pure copper often preferred to brass for electrical wiring?
options: It generally has higher electrical conductivity and good ductility.
questions.explanation: Alloying commonly trades some conductivity for other useful properties.

questions.prompt: Does the simple distorted-lattice picture predict every alloy property quantitatively?
options: Yes; any drawing gives an exact strength.
Yes; all alloys have identical hardness.
No alloy contains a crystal structure.
No; composition, phases and processing also influence properties.
questions.explanation: The model explains a mechanism but is not a complete material-performance calculation.
